speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: STATEMENT ON FIXED COMBINATIONS OF ANTIBIOTICS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a result of several inquiries, mainly from the hon. member for Winnipeg North, I wish to make a statement concerning antibiotics and their labelling.
Several announcements have been made recently by the United States Food and Drug Administration that certain combination drug 21545-12^
products will be removed from the market This action was based on reports from the drug efficacy study group established by the U.S. National Academy of Sciences-National Research Council that products containing fixed combinations of antibiotics are ineffective for claims made in their labelling.
We are well aware that fixed-ratio drug formulations have been the subject of controversy in medical circles for some years. However, in spite of the opinions expressed in the U.S.A., there are some physicians who believe that these combinations are of value and would wish them to be retained on the market. The debate as to whether fixed-ratio combinations should be prescribed is a matter which properly rests with the medical profession.
Nevertheless, some months ago the Food and Drug Directorate, Department of National Health and Welfare, initiated discussions with Canadian manufacturers of certain antibiotic combinations. If these investigations show the need, manufacturers will be required to include additional explanatory or cautionary information on the label of the drug or in the professional literature accompanying the drug or being supplied to the professions. If evidence is obtained that these combinations are less effective than their individual components or if they are found to represent a hazard to health, the directorate will take further appropriate action.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
The directorate has authority under Section 9(1) of the Food and Drugs Act to prevent the sale of a drug product that is labelled in a manner that is false, misleading or deceptive in regard to its merit or safety.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON FIXED COMBINATIONS OF ANTIBIOTICS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the minister for giving me advance notice of this statement. I am glad he has realized there has been a mild controversy in medical circles for a good many years about fixed combinations of antibiotics. Those who work in universities and hospitals tend to believe that there should not be combinations while those who are involved with the general care of the public have often thought that in certain cases these fixed combinations are of value.
1298	COMMONS
Minister's Statement on Antibiotics
I agree with the minister that he has gone carefully and slowly, and I believe that in certain conditions physicians would agree that fixed combinations of antibiotics are useful, particularly in a widely scattered country. However, we have to recognize that medical technology is advancing With regard to the desirable role of specific drugs for specific conditions. This is being brought closer and the use of fixed combinations of antibiotics will decrease in the future. I believe that the Food and Drug Directorate has done well not to ban these combinations immediately as has been done in the United States. I look with interest to further evidence as to what the department will do.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON FIXED COMBINATIONS OF ANTIBIOTICS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to note how long it took the minister to make the statement he made today, a statement in which he really said nothing. In other instances, such as auto safety and the use of cyclamates, we in Canada have waited for United States agencies to take action and have then followed their action and took their advice on the basis of the tests they have conducted.
In this case the minister decided to listen to the drug industry and to ignore the findings of the United States agency which made a very careful study of the problem taking more than three years and costing over $1 million. This study was conducted by the United States National Academy of Sciences-National Research Council.
They found that two-thirds of the prescription drugs used in the United States are badly labelled and a large percentage are partly or totally ineffective. They found, in a study of 4,000 drug preparations, 85 per cent of them prescription drugs supplied by over 200 firms, that 7 per cent were totally ineffective. Others were found effective for some diseases and partly or not at all for others for which effectiveness was claimed. The study showed that two-thirds of the drugs were poorly organized, repetitive, out of date, evasive and promotionally oriented. They ordered a large number of prescription drugs to be relabelled and called for the banning of sales of 54 specific drugs.
In light of their findings it is disappointing, to say the least, to find the minister making a statement in which he in effect says that the government is not prepared to do anything. This does not surprise me, Mr. Speaker. We have watched this government over a period of four or five years make extensive studies of drug safety and drug prices and come up with proposals which have had little, if any,

DEBATES	November 27. 1969
effect in improving drug safety and no effect on drug prices. All the steps taken led to no changes in the very high prices of drugs.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON FIXED COMBINATIONS OF ANTIBIOTICS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am wondering if this statement is not related to a recent decision taken by the Americans in connection with the ban On germ warfare.
In any event, it is a statement which tells us what the Department of National Health and Welfare intends to do with regard to drugs. In this statement, we find that if evidence is obtained that combinations are less effective than their individual components, the Director General of the Food and Drug Directorate will take the steps needed to remedy the situation.
Mr. Speaker, as the previous speakers, I rejoice in the position taken because the drug industry is different from others, first because experience has taught me that drugs have more frequently been used to make money than to cure, and also, at the manufacturing level, this industry sets selling prices which are in no way prorated to costs. We have a right to have doubts about the value of what is contained in drugs.
Therefore, I congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) who, by his attitude, will contribute, in my opinion, to restrain the shameful exploitation of the sick and the old.

In this particular instance the decision on whether a prosecution should be taken properly lies with the Montreal authorities or with the Attorney General of Quebec. The right hon. gentleman is talking about subversion, sedition and this sort of thing, and quite properly so. I have searched the records and at no time since Confederation has a prosecution for sedition been taken by the federal Attorney General. Sedition is a crime under the Criminal Code of Canada and in this, as in all other matters, prosecutions taken under the Criminal Code are taken by the provincial Attorneys General.
The only two cases I could find in the last 30 years relating to sedition were both taken against the Jehovah's Witnesses by the Attorney General of Quebec. The only cases of sedition currently before the courts, the one against Michel Chartrand, the one against Pierre Valiere and the one that was dismissed against Charles Gagnon, were also taken by the Attorney General of Quebec. speechtext:

He said: Mr. Speaker, first of all may I express my regret at the absence, through illness, of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp). We had hoped he could participate in this debate and hope he will have a speedy recovery from his illness.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NIGERIA-BIAFRA- ALLEGED FAILURE TO TAKE MEASURES TO RELIEVE STARVATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NIGERIA-BIAFRA- ALLEGED FAILURE TO TAKE MEASURES TO RELIEVE STARVATION
speechtext:
As hon. members of the House are aware, this day has designated "Peace in Biafra Day". Across Canada many Canadians are considering the plight of their fellow human beings in Nigeria and Biafra who, as

DEBATES	November 27, 1969
the House well knows, as a result of a stalemated war are threatened with mass starvation. It seems to me entirely appropriate that this House, representing as it does all the people of Canada, should devote its time in an effort to determine whether more can be done to aid the prospective victims of starvation in those unfortunate areas.
There are two points on which I think all members of the House will agree. First, that the security of all of us depends on the creation of a world community in which basic human rights, and the most fundamental of all, the right to life, are respected. Second, that though Nigeria and Biafra seem remote to many Canadians, we are right to be concerned about the tragic fate facing many innocent victims of the war and right to do all within our power to relieve their plight. Where we differ is on what can be done and how it should be done. The motion which Your Honour put to the House contends that the government has not done enough in this field.
I ask these questions: What has it done, what has it left undone; what has it failed to do that in our opinions should have been done; and what can be done in future? I intend to be entirely specific in the answers I give those questions. Indeed, the motion itself is specific.
The government could have assisted the Joint Church Aid operations by providing aircraft and/or supplies and/or money. It has failed to do so. The motion urges that it do so in future.
First, Mr. Speaker, let us review what the government has done. On October 24, as indicated at page 37 of Hansard, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that the government had contributed $3 million towards food and relief supplies to be distributed in Biafra. If the Prime Minister takes part in this debate I shall be interested in hearing how that $3 million was divided. How much was spent on the federal side of the lines, and how much on the other side.
In October, 1968, the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) and I returned from a brief visit to Biafra. We pleaded with the government at that time to make Canadian Hercules aircraft available both to the International Red Cross, which was operating an airlift from Fernando Po to Uli airport, Biafra, and to the church operations which later became known as Joint Church Aid, which had aircraft operating to the same airstrip at Uli from the island of Sao Tome. If
November 27, 1969

the government had accepted our request at that time the amount of supplies flowing to the beleaguered areas of Biafra would have been doubled. The government could have saved the lives of many hundred of thousands of people who made up part of the estimated 1.5 million people who have died of starvation in the area since then. The same plea on behalf of the International Red Cross was made by the Canadian Red Cross High Commissioner, Major-General Wrinch. But what happened?
The government dispatched a grand total of three Hercules aircraft to Nigeria and Biafra. They did not stay very long. The first aircraft left for Lagos on October 10, 1968. It was permanently grounded in Lagos until it returned to Canada a few weeks later. The pretext advanced for not using this aircraft was that two of the airstrips in the federally occupied territories were in a poor state of repair and that the Hercules aircraft would damage the runways. The other airfield available was being used, according to Nigerian authorities, for military purposes and therefore was not available. Mr. Speaker, one of these airports was Calabar, an internationally recognized airport. Hercules aircraft are supposed to be able to land in open fields. Actually, a Hercules aircraft did land at the improvised airstrip at Uli, in Biafra. The Canadian officer in charge of the operation expressed mystification about the alleged landing difficulties. The plain fact is that Nigerian government does not seem to have been interested, and there does not appear to have been any protest on the part of the Canadian government that the aircraft was not used in that region.
Another Canadian Hercules aircraft was dispatched on October 15, 1968, to Fernando Po, to assist in the airlift of the International Red Cross from that island to Uli. It made ten flights to Uli with about 200 tons of food. Most of the time the aircraft was grounded, and in about December of the same year, 1968, it returned to Canada where it has remained ever since. The third aircraft was merely a supply aircraft and need not be counted.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
The reason given for withdrawing the effort was that one of the church operated aircraft had been shot at, and that the operation had become too dangerous. Nevertheless, the church operations continued. A second reason given by the Prime Minister in this
Alleged Failure to Aid Biafrans House about a year ago was that the Biafran authorities would not accept daylight flights proposed by the Nigerian federal government. The Prime Minister made clear that this condition was made, that General Ojukwu would undertake not to use the airstrip during the daylight hours for arms shipments Here, we get the very first proposal of daylight flights subject to conditions of military significance. The condemnation of General Ojukwu as the obstructor of relief for his own people is used as an excuse for inaction. I will have more to say about this later.
The more we look into why this particular reason (the question of daylight flights) is being advanced and nothing being done, the more we see it is not an adequate or proper reason. I will explain my reason for this statement later. I would like to say if there were no daylight flights bringing arms into Uli, which General Ojukwu was asked to forgo, both the condition by the Nigerians and the refusal of the Biafrans are absolutely senseless. There is no point in asking for the condition nor any point in denying the condition. It is perfectly obvious that was not the purpose. There were in fact air flights coming in with arms and therefore the request had a military significance. If such flights were taking place bringing arms into Uli, General Ojukwu, hard-pressed in a war which he and the people he led thought was a war of extermination, was being asked to surrender his means of defence or in effect to surrender, period.
Of course, the Nigerians knew and I think others, including the Prime Minister, should have recognized that such an offer with this condition was bound to be refused. When it was refused he should have known that it was really a propaganda device, a device that unfortunately has been all too successful in alienating sympathy, not from the Biafran regime-that is not important perhaps-but from the innocent victims of the war.
As I have said, this Canadian effort through the three Hercules lasted a few weeks. It delivered to Biafra 200 tons in 10 flights. I want the House to compare that with the results of the operations of the churches which we, in this motion, are asking the House to support. The joint church operation, apart from the International Red Cross, of which Canairelief, the Canadian agency mentioned in the motion, is an agency and important component had at the end of October last flown 4,183 flights and delivered 45,000 tons of food and supplies into Uli. Yet the Canadian government effort is 200 tons compared
1310	COMMONS
Alleged Failure to Aid Biafrans with the churches and voluntary agencies 45,000 tons. There have been 10 government flights as against 4,183 church sponsored flights.
Since June, 1969 when an International Red Cross plane was shot down by the Nigerian air force in broad daylight, with its clear Red Cross emblem oh it, the International Red Cross has ceased to operate. The joint church-aid operation has carried on, despite hazardous conditions and the loss of lives of crew members and planes, and is flying on night operations on the average of 15 flights a night, bringing in approximately 200 tons a night. This is not enough, Mr. Speaker. It is estimated the need to cope with starvation is approximately 500 tons a night, but nevertheless it is a substantial and magnificent contribution and the only organization doing an effective job at the moment. I submit it deserves the support of this country and this government.
It is this operation that the motion before the House asks the government to support. So far, the government has persistently refused to contribute. Yet that operation, together with the International Red Cross, is estimated to have saved three million lives and if given the tools and the means will save many hundreds of thousands of lives in the future. If we condemn this government, it is because it failed to support this operation and does not support it to the present time.
I want to examine some of the reasons for the refusal of the government. I will state them as fairly as I can and ask the Prime Minister and the House to consider very carefully whether these refusals are justified by the reasons I advance. In my view, they do not constitute valid grounds for refusal of assistance. They are pretexts rather than good grounds. I am sure the government holds some of its views with great sincerity, but I think if they will only look again, and look carefully, they will find them to be without substance. What are the objections? I will first list them and then deal with them in order to show why they are not valid objections.
First, it is said that the Biafran regime ought to accept daylight flights, but has refused, presumably out of sheer perversity, and is therefore the party primarily responsible for the starvation of the people. Second, it is said that the International Red Cross is the designated international agency for mercy operations of this kind and that this government can operate only through it.

DEBATES	November 27, 1969
Third, it is said that the Nigerian federal government, which is the sovereign authority over the whole area, will not consent to the joint church-aid operations and that to assist these flights would be an unjustifiable intervention contrary to the sovereignty of Nigeria. Sometimes it is put in more extravagant language. The Prime Minister said it would be an act of war. Fourth, it is said that General Ojukwu and the Biafreins are secessionists and rebels, and that nothing must be done to aid or encourage such breakaway regimes.
I propose to deal with each of these objections one at a time. The first is that the Biafran regime has refused to accept daylights flights and that this refusal is unreasonable and unjustifiable. This bald statement as it stands is not true, Mr. Speaker. Both the Nigerian and Biafran governments have accepted in principle the International Red Cross proposals for daylight flights. Both have found conditions proposed by the other side unacceptable.
I have in my hands a document containing proposals for relief flights by the International Red Cross to Uli and the document points out that it is as agreed by Professor Freymond and Dr. Cookey who represents the International Red Cross. The document is dated August 27 last. It is based upon the proposals of the International Red Cross of August 1. It provides for a controlling commission of representatives of a neutral state appointed by the federal military government of Nigeria and the Biafran authorities. The bases were to be Cotonou and Santa Isabel. It provides for detailed routings and corridors, for all aircraft to be identified by Red Cross emblems and that Nigerian air space can only be entered after nine o'clock in the morning and after six o'clock in the evening.
Apparently this proposal was unacceptable to the federal government. The Red Cross entered into a second document, which I also have here, this time agreeable to the federal military government, but unacceptable to the Biafrans. It excluded any representative of a neutral state appointed by the Biafran authorities. The host state, the federal military government and the International Red Cross were to be the commissioners. The operations was moved to Cotonou and Santa Isabel was ruled out.
All flights and routing emblems, etc., were to be agreed on by the International Red Cross with the Nigerian air force and the Nigerian army. It seems this provision would
November 27, 1969

give complete control or at least a veto power over the flights to the federal military government's authorities. The flight time was cut down from nine a.m. to five p.m. Article 6(2) provided that this agreement was to be without prejudice to the military operations of the federal military government.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
The agreement was to last for three weeks only. It is in return for this agreement that it is suggested the Biafran regime should surrender, or at least discourage, the night flights which were bringing them in infinitely more than this proposed Red Cross flight could possibly have done. The Uli airport is a small strip which can receive only a limited number of flights. Under the present set-up operated by the joint churches it is used for approximately 13J hours, and some 25 flights come in each night. Some of these, no doubt, bring in arms. It is proposed by the federal military government in the International Red Cross agreement to cut down the period of daylight flights to eight hours. In effect, the Nigerian government is trying to discourage the night flights, which have been highly effective, in favour of a daylight program which they could control. How could anyone seriously doubt that such an agreement would have military implications? Yet the Prime Minister has given the Biafran refusal to accept this agreement as a reason for withholding aid from Biafra.
It is said that the Biafran government asked for military guarantees and then turned down reasonable proposals by the United States government and other countries. This should be looked into again. As I understand it, the Biafrans claim that the guarantees they want are guarantees of the security of Uli airport, their one lifeline and vital means of survival. It is not enough, they say, to guarantee, as has been proposed, that the IRC flights should not be used for military purposes. I do not suppose it was expected they would be. It seems to me this whole situation should be looked into carefully again.
Let us suppose, however, that the Biafran authorities are unduly suspicious of the intention of the federal military government to use daylight flights to their advantage. Is this surprising? They have been the victims of pogroms, massive expulsion, blockade, starvation, aerial bombardment of schools, hospitals, market places and other civilian targets. It is
Alleged Failure to Aid Biafrans not reasonable to expect them to agree to anything which might lead to military defeat, as they fear extermination.
The second objection taken by the Canadian government to assisting this relief effort on the lines I have mentioned is that Canada recognizes the ancient and honourable tradition of the International Red Cross in the field of mercy operations during wartime. The government points out that international recognition has been given to that organization. This is not an unreasonable argument, but the Prime Minister himself, in his speech of October 24 to which I have referred, suggested it would have to be looked into again. Since June 5 no Red Cross flights have taken place at all, nor does there seem to be any reasonable prospect of their resumption. It is the joint church-aid program which is flying out supplies by night. This organization is no fly-by-night organization-

speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NIGERIA-BIAFRA- ALLEGED FAILURE TO TAKE MEASURES TO RELIEVE STARVATION
speechtext:
I did not intend to make a pun. It is true the organization does fly by night. It is supported by 27 church organizations, including the World Council of Churches, Caritas International, representing the Roman Catholic Church, and many other religious bodies. It is international; it is ecumenical, and it is doing a job. I think it deserves support. These church groups are not politically minded; they are committed to work of compassion and mercy. They operate on both sides of the line. If we can assist the International Red Cross when it is not in operation, surely we can help the churches in their task of mercy.
The third objection states that the Nigerian federal government is the sovereign authority over the whole area and will not consent to the church operation. It is claimed that to assist these flights would therefore be an unjustifiable intervention, even an act of war. But the right of humanitarian intervention in certain circumstances, even in the face of opposition by the nation state, has been recognized in law for centuries by many authorities. I shall spare the House a lengthy recital of those authorities but I wish to give some examples, on the basis of which I urge the government to reconsider its position. One is Ronald St. John Macdonald, dean of the Toronto Law School and Canadian representative at the third session of the United Nations 20th General Assembly. Dean Macdonald prepared a paper or memorandum on
November 27, 1969

Alleged Failure to Aid Biafrans this important subject for a committee of this House, the External Affairs Committee, and from this memorandum I extract only the following clear statement:
It is lawful for Canada to assist church agencies in sending food and medical supplies into Biafra.
Dean Macdonald is not one who speaks on such a matter lightly. Next, I want to read an excerpt from the review of the International Commission of Jurists written as recently as June, 1969, in which it is stated:
In law as in fact, the conflict in Nigeria can no longer be regarded as a matter of purely national concern. The proportions it has reached and its significance in the decline of international standards and the violation of human rights require that it be solved as a matter of priority by the international community. Although previous efforts have failed, the United Nations, as the only collective organ of this community, could perhaps still take positive action.
Finally, as far as the legal aspect of the matter is concerned, I wish to refer to an article written by Professor Reisman of the Yale Law School. He said this:
To summarize, international policy even before Grotius has been firmly and continuously for humanitarian intervention in those extreme cases where the most minimal of human rights were in jeopardy. Forceful intervention in such circumstances in the territory of another state is permissible and, for the signatories of the Charter and the Genocide Convention, is mandatory. The effect of the United Nations ha$ been to develop a coordinate set of competence. In circumstances in which an authoritative organ of the UN or of a relevant regional organization can either not act or not act with sufficient dispatch, individual or coordinated collective non-UN humanitarian intervention is permitted as a substitute or functional enforcement of international human rights.
So much for the argument that there is no right of intervention. There is really no excuse for inaction on our part. It is somewhat ironical to hear it suggested that we cannot give this aid because it would amount to an act of war. If this were so, the United States, West Germany, Sweden, The Netherlands and other countries, which have given aid to joint church programs would be at war with the federal government of Nigeria. But as far as I know, they are not. The aid has been given directly and indirectly to joint church assistance programs.
The aid provided by the United States government has been very substantial The United States sold four stratofreighters to joint church-aid and four to the International Red Cross for $4,000 each, or their scrap value. This aircraft is similar in capacity to the Hercules which the Canadian government 
would not make available to Canairelief or joint church-aid. In addition, the United States government has been making tonnage payments to church agencies flying relief supplies into Biafra, and this has greatly assisted Canairelief. It is ironical that the Canadian government should refuse to support a Canadian relief agency which is receiving substantial support indirectly from the United States government. Surely, the position of the Canadian government here is legalistic and not realistic.
The last objection to doing anything about this matter is that Colonel Ojukwu and the Biafran secessionists are rebels who should not be assisted even indirectly. If this be true, they were indeed reluctant secessionists, reluctant rebels. They were in effect thrown out of the federation by force. Efforts are now being made to force them back in again. They have fought valiantly for two years against superior odds for self-determination and the right to survive. I suggest in any event that judgments of censure in these circumstances, even if they are justified, are not the overriding factor. Political considerations do not justify denial of human concern and intervention by the peoples of the world.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
The motion which we have introduced concludes with an appeal or invitation to the government to change its policy and provide assistance to Joint church-aid or, if it prefers, through Canairelief. It seems to me that the Prime Minister has left the door open. In his speech during the debate on the throne speech he made it quite clear, as reported at pages 37 and 38 of Hansard, that if other methods did not succeed new methods would be examined. Even in the rather harshly worded statement that he made on Tuesday of this week, the Prime Minister did not close the door.
We in this comer of the House would be extremely happy to withdraw this motion, which does imply some censure of the government, if the Prime Minister were to announce that the government would extend assistance to the starving people of Biafra through the only available operative agency, joint church-aid and Canairelief. I can assure the House that we seek no partisan benefit out of this tragic affair.
Every day, Mr. Speaker, you or whoever is in the Chair repeat to us the words from the Lord's Prayer "Give us this day our daily bread". Today perhaps the people of Nigeria
November 27, 1969

and Biafra are saying to us in their hour of tragedy "Give us this day our daily bread". To the extent that it is within our power, we must respond. It is our belief-and this is the reason we have put forward this motion-that it is within our power to respond, and that the motion points the way to an effective response.

speechtext: The answer is simple, Mr. Speaker. The answer is yes. I know that the leader of this party has communicated with the leader of the British government and clearly expressed his distress at the actions of that government. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NIGERIA-BIAFRA- ALLEGED FAILURE TO TAKE MEASURES TO RELIEVE STARVATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, usually one comment about the illness of a colleague is enough because we can all share it; but since there is a long list of speakers and we are caught in the system, as it were, may I with no less sincerity say that we of the official opposition are also sorry to hear of the illness of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) and hope that he will soon recover. I think he had a very arduous trip to the Near East, and like a good many others in public life he is paying the price for this type of intense personal involvement in world problems.
This, sadly, is the resumption of what might be called an adjourned debate. My leader raised the issue of aid in the Nigerian civil war as his first question in the first
Alleged Failure to Aid Biafrans session of the 28th parliament. Since that time both the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and members on both sides of the House have relentlessly pursued this issue.
May I say at the outset that the members of the official opposition support, without equivocation the motion that has been proposed by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), since it presents a very easy- in the straight sense and meaning of that word-formula to enable the government to give direct assistance without getting into any nuances of diplomacy.
The last time that the House formally discussed the issue, journalists described the contribution I made as being emotional. Much as I have tried to drain any emotion from my speech in a debate dealing with a tragedy like this, I fear I will once again be open to the same criticism. I do not know how man is supposed to go through life untouched by human tragedy, unmoved by death or by a civil war that is so unnecessary.
Today the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has received a good many petitions. Those of us who are trying to revamp the system, to use such phrases as participatory democracy and other terms relating to responsiveness to government and to people's feelings, have been touched by the really national concern that has been so manifest today, a special day of peace for Nigeria and Biafra.
I have before me a rather unique petition in that it is signed by a good many religious leaders of this country and is also supported by people of no religion. This petition I will read because the record should be complete:
We, the undersigned, appeal to the Government of Canada and to concerned people everywhere to bring political pressure to bear on those countries- amongst them the United Kingdom, the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics and France, to do all in their power to end the supply of arms to Nigeria and Biafra, and to bring both sides to the conference table to begin the search for a lasting peace and a solution based on the will of the people.
We draw to the attention of Governments the appeals made by His Holiness the Pope and the World Council of Churches, also the resolution passed at the Labour Party Conference at Brighton September. 1969 calling for international action.
The hon. member for Greenwood referred to the statement made in June, 1969 by the International Commission of Jurists, so I will not repeat it. This statement is included in the petition.
We recognize that this is an African problem which will be solved by Africa but we are convinced that before this can happen outside pressures in the form of arms and finance must be cut
1314	COMMONS
Alleged Failure to Aid Biafrans
off. In the name of two million dead and in the name of those who still survive we call for an end to all action that prolongs this conflict and urge men everywhere to think first and foremost of those in direct need of food, shelter and medical care.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
This is a letter supported by the signatures of thousands of Canadians and it is signed by Most Reverend Philip J. Pocock, Co-Adjutor and Archbishop of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Toronto; the Most Reverend H. H. Clark, Primate of the Anglican Church of Canada; Dr. Robert B. McClure, Moderator of the United Church of Canada; the Very Reverend D. H. Johnson, Moderator of the Presbyterian Church of Canada and Rabbi W. G. Plaut of the Holy Blossom Temple. It was dated Toronto, October 10. I felt it worthwhile to include this letter in my few comments because I feel it is really the focus of what this day is all about.
Herbert Gold, who was writing in the November issue of Harper's magazine, said:
Biafra makes bad dreams for people who refuse to dream.
"Hunger is a legitimate weapon of war", says one of the Nigerian generals, as the statesmen of the world rely on the end coming before they need make up their minds about the issues. This is a tragic indictment to have to make but this is part of what is happening in the United Kingdom. That country feels a unique responsibility for Nigeria. The Labour party at its meeting has repudiated the Government's action in this regard. The London Times in an editorial November 18, just a week or so ago states:
-if Britain was exercising a strict limit to arms supplies, she would be in a much stronger position to bring (as Sir Alec Douglas-Home suggests) the other suppliers, notably Russia and France, to a conference on the withholding of arms from both sides.
This opportunity, like so many others, has been lost, while the Government has equivocated. Whatever their problems in Lagos, Mr. Wilson and Mr. Stewart should realize that Britain stands in an especially vulnerable moral position over Biafra. It is essential that they should now not only put a ceiling on supplies but should reconsider their whole policy of maintaining them. The least they now owe to British opinion is a new and sincere effort to bring about a political settlement.
The truth is that Mr. Stewart's policy has been wrong at every stage. Again and again the false expectation of "the quick kill" has persuaded the government to continue arms, to continue as the munitions men when they should have been the conciliators. Both sides in Nigeria bear a terrible responsibility for this war; so does Russia, whose synicism is total and unredeemed; so does the British government.

DEBATES	November 27, 1969
I think of all the indictments this is the most telling-waiting for the quick kill; the world standing aside unable to act, the United Nations using such phrases as "an internal matter" after 2J years and 2 million dead. I really do not see why any young person should not wonder and get a bit hung-up about some of our institutions, both national and international, if this is the way we respond.
One of the most interesting statements on the whole issue was made by one Renata Adler in the October 4 edition of the New Yorker. She tells about asking a young Bia-fran, "Just whose children it is who are dying"? He replied quite seriously that it is the children of villagers who are not strong enough to trek near the front to buy what food there is more cheaply and trek back to market to sell it more dearly, for a little profit to support their families. It takes a high tolerance for the sheer, bitterly comic ugliness of human suffering to care much for these survivors out of the Bertolt Brecht.
Editorial writers for the western press, unlike reporters on the spot, often treat the Biafran position as morally ambiguous, as though the years from 1939 to 1945 had never existed, and as though killing and dying existed on a single plane of atrocity. It is possible that another ethnic population will be decimated before modern intelligence completes its debate about the extent to which the greatest crimes can be said to be the fault of the victims of them.
I obviously do not indict the government on this issue. I indict the representatives and all of us in whatever country we may be. 1 do indict the Government, however, for its failure to respond to the obvious need and request that has been made, with lots of time for consideration by the Government.
The point that has troubled me is the unrealness of much of the discussion; the withdrawal of world leadership behind fixed and, I regret to say, stereotyped positions. What would have happened if joint church-aid had spent its time arguing about who was at fault, who was to blame? What would be the toll now if joint church-aid had awaited the pleasure of the United Nations or begged admission to either parts of Nigeria from the Organization of African Unity?
I say again this unreality is symptomatic of our times, and I believe very sincerely that it accounts for much of the alienation, to use an ugly word, of so many people from our leadership, our systems and institutions. I admit it
November 27, 1969

takes a far tougher hide than mine to have the atrocities of this tragic war share the few moments on the television news, and then have our leadership ask those who feel that help should be given to go through the proper and orthodox channels. It surprises me very much that in this era the Government is taken aback by the number of people who want something done.
I read, because it was short, the speech made at Sir George Williams yesterday by the Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans) about participatory democracy. As a member of the administration he understands something about feedback. I suggest that the whole effect today is the result of the massive feedback the government is getting about the frustration of the citizens of this country regarding inactivity in the field of aid to joint church-aid.
I also believe sincerely that a good deal of the trouble, and here I may be on dangerous ground and others may shoot me down for it, in the world today is brought about by what I may call sterile ideological debate. These are the sort of positions that are taken. I listened to a debate of this type the other day at the United Nations on the China issue. You put your hand in a slot and out comes the same speech that has been repeated every year for the last 15 or 20 years. How in heavens name do you expect the practical issues facing man to be solved if there is no softening of the positions?
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
For making such a statement as this at a conference, not at Harrison Hot Springs, I was said to be soft on Communism. May I repeat that unreal discussions seem to be going on which have no relevancy to the problem that we are facing. The problem is hunger, starvation and death. The means are there to alleviate hunger, starvation and death and we are doing a sort of minuet about sovereignty. I hope the Prime Minister will tell us why it has not been possible until now to give help to joint church aid and its agent Canairelief. As the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) and I have said- and I will repeat it-they are doing the job now. This is the only source of food and medicine for Biafra. The International Committee of the Red Cross has not flown a plane since mid-June. I suppose if I wanted to do so I could start a moral condemnation of this attitude, but what good would it do? I will say this; Canada has taken initiative. I think
Alleged Failure to Aid Biafrans it was at Istanbul, or at the recent meeting of the ICRC, that a formula for relief was suggested that would be part of the covenant of nations, in other words, exercising the right of innocent victims of war. I hope very much that this will take effect. I think the avenue for the government to follow is at hand. I believe it is really quite bitterly ironic that Canairelief is to such a large degree funded by the United States government and funds from several countries in Europe.
I believe it is irony compounded that Canairelief may be forced to close down its relief operations because of the withdrawal of the support of the United States government, as a result of the indifference of this government. May I add that while the government has been unable to act, today the hon. member for Greenwood and myself, as directors of Canairelief, were recipients of $28,000 from the Ottawa branch of the Miles for Millions. I think this is a commendable act on behalf of that charity.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NIGERIA-BIAFRA- ALLEGED FAILURE TO TAKE MEASURES TO RELIEVE STARVATION
speechtext:
I want to pay this public tribute to that organization. It is a pity that there is a bit of polarization in this Parliament in respect of this issue. I cannot believe, if this motion is voted upon, that there will be party positions taken on a human tragedy such as this. I do not believe, when I walk down the corridor with a friend and colleague from the government, that his view and my view are very different about wanting to do something. Are we to believe that government supporters are any less moved than the other members in the House by the tragedy the world faces? Truly, the world faces this tragedy.
Is party solidarity so necessary that a member would allow it to stifle his concern? Mr. Speaker, there is so much that could be said about this issue. In the article in the New Yorker there is a most interesting philosophical discussion of the whole issue-perhaps "issue" is not the word-the whole case of the world standing by to watch. The world stood watching too many times in this century. The world debated whether matters were internal or external from 1932 to 1945. I, for one, am not prepared to have it said that this House or even this government, because it is the government of Canada, was unable to act because a matter was an internal matter. We must be flexible enough to deal with the issue. The issue, as has been said, is relief and
November 27, 1969

Alleged Failure to Aid Biafrans how to get it to those who need it. We can use the same flexibility in dealing with relief for Biafra that the Canadian Wheat Board, for instance, is using now in its dealings with the Peoples Republic of China, a government which we do not recognize. Nobody is doing a song and dance about that.
I am informed that a group of church leaders from Winnipeg has written to the Prime Minister asking him to appoint a mission to visit both sides in Nigeria and Biafra. The suggestion of these gentlemen is that Mr. Lester Pearson, who has a world-wide reputation, would be an obvious choice to head such a group. I received a bit of flak for making such a dangerous suggestion during the last debate. Surely, it is an initiative which might be recommended. The only qualification I would have is that the world is asking so much of Mr. Pearson at this stage. Jim Hoag-land in last evening's edition of the Montreal Star, in an article entitled "Brinkmanship in Nigerian war", spoke of the mutual distrust. This is something which I think a really authentic or legitimate mission, if that is the expression, sent by the government of Canada could help alleviate. Mr. Hoagland said:
The deadlock on talks at a time when they should be moving ahead seems to illustrate two important factors in the war that is Africa's agony:
Neither side feels it can believe the other. The confusion over Biafra's November statements was matched by the incongruous incident of September, in which Nigeria's leader, Maj. Gen. Yakubu Gowon, said Nigeria would accept talks without pre-conditions, only to have his information minister, Anthony Enahoro, say two days later that Nigeria would not accept such talks.
If I might interpolate here, I think this too has been one of the problems in this country; that is, that Gowon, although a major-general and head of a military government is in effect a "captive" of more hawkish people within his cabinet. The article continues:
Many analysts interpreted this as confirmation of a long rumoured split within the Nigerian leadership, with Gowon being in the dove camp that wants talks and Enahoro speaking for the hawks.
The distrustful Biafrans will not accept even this possibility. Ojukwu's top advisers say the incident was carefully orchestrated to give the impression of Gowon wanting peace while doing nothing to obtain it.
Neither side feels weak enough to bargain. The week following Ojukwu's press conference saw major air attacks by the Biafrans, which are likely to bolster the Biafran hopes that they can hold out until the Nigerians are willing to negotiate.
The Nigerians retaliated, according to reliable reports, by resuming bombing of civilian areas in Biafra, and are capable of greatly intensifying such bombing if goaded into it.

Lagos also does not feel that it should gamble on losing at the peace table what it has won on the battlefield. The Nigerians are confident that, at the least, they can contain the Biafrans in the small enclave, and wait for them to crack.
A visitor to both sides recently can see some of the frightening logic in each position. But the fruits of this logic are likely to become even more bitter for each side, unless meaningful talks are started-now.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful for the minute or two the House has graciously given me. I keep saying this each time I receive consent to continue although it shoots down my argument for shorter speeches. However, I think we were very interested to read just yesterday about the initiative taken by Biafra to ask Switzerland and several other neutral countries of Europe to mediate a cease-fire. I think this is a significant development, but it does not change the need for humanitarian aid forthwith.

I believe that the matter under consideration affects many Canadians, and not only politicians or churchmen, but also citizens interested in foreign affairs.
Last year, the house instructed the Committee on External Affairs and National Defence to inquire into the Nigeria-Biafra tragedy. I myself was on that committee which heard several experts about the situation prevailing there.
Following that inquiry there was a debate in the house. In fact, the two previous speakers made recommendations to the government which dealt mostly with disarmament.
Mr. Speaker, no doubt there is a civil war going on there. It is not a war between two foreign countries but one between the people of the same country. Corneille had written that "civil war is the realm of crime".
Undoubtedly in Nigeria, not only on the battlefields but also elsewhere, tragedies are played out and grudges are paid off.

In a war of this type the problem is always the same, i.e., providing for the ones who are not directly involved. Indeed getting supplies to the soldiers is of paramount importance for the country. I think that General Gowon's as well as Colonel Ojukwu's first concern is to supply his forces. Old people, women, children, and generally people who are not on the battlefield are looked after last.
And the necessary steps are taken on both sides so that supplies will not reach enemy forces to strengthen them.
The war that is opposing Biafra to Nigeria is not different from other wars. It will cause insurmountable problems as long as the two parties involved do not, through negotiations, find a way to end this conflict which has lasted much too long already.
We have been advocating such negotiations between Nigeria and Biafra, but until now without any really effective result. We have been told that Colonel Ojukwu has asked recently for assistance from Switzerland, a country whose neutrality is well known and whose interventions are often successful in seltling disputes between some countries.
Apparently, it is expected that the reply of Switzerland will be consistent with its traditional policy. The Bern government would be willing to offer its services if the two opposing parties so desired and if the mediation had any chance of succeeding.
But now one country is requested to act as a mediator in order to reach a settlement while conditions are imposed that make any agreement impossible.
Therefore, I wonder whether the two leaders in this war have any sense of responsibility.
The UNESCO Constitution states, and I quote:
As wars originate in the minds of men, it is in the minds of men that peace must build its defences.
I believe that it is on the two leaders that pressure must be exerted in order to bring this war to an end.
The government is asked to supply more food, more medical products and more supplies of all kinds to help the starving. That is

An agreement should be reached on the necessity of a real truce in order to bring to a stop the hardship that is prevalent in that part of the world.
The dispute between the two countries has not only to do with the fact that the Nigerians want to protect their interests. Foreign financial interests are also involved.
During the inquiry made by the Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, it was recognized that oil interests had contributed to the start of the slaughter which is taking place in this part of Africa.
Last year at the interparliamentary conference in Lima, a representative of Switzerland, precisely the country which is asked to act as mediator, said, and I quote:
Economic and political interests are lurking behind this fatal aid.
Without military assistance from Great Britain, the Soviet Union and a few other countries, the military government of Lagos would have been unable to launch a war against the Ibos.
As for Biafra, it is not much better. France and Portugal also favour the secession to protect their own interests. By supporting Biafra, they hope to obtain some right on the oil resources of the Delta and the Niger. It is urgent to stop sending arms to either parties; to protect economic and political interests by supplying arms is one of the forms of neo-colonialism.
Mr. Speaker, in November 1968, when we dealt with the matter in this House, the Conservative member who has just resumed his seat moved, seconded by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), and I quote:
That the Canadian government, alone or in conjunction with like-minded countries, should take initiatives to persuade nations supplying arms to the combatants in Nigeria-Biafra to stop the flow of arms without which the war would soon no longer be possible.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know to what extent the Canadian government has put the pressure on to stop the delivery of arms to the belligerent forces in this war. But it is no secret that that country is unable, by itself, to set up the industries needed to produce the arms used in the slaughter. Such arms, therefore, come from outside.
The first thing to consider, if we want to end this conflict, is that the delivery of arms to both parties must be stopped so as to make

Mr. Speaker, today we received a lecture in the form of an alibi. Is the government of Canada going to contribute to Canairelief? The answer is that it is not. That was quite definitely stated, though it was suggested that following 18 months of consideration on the part of the government the government is still considering ways and means that might be taken.
Let me recall what happened in the city of Halifax when the Prime Minister was asked by a group of students whether he would do something on behalf of the poor people of Biafra. The Prime Minister's reply was: "Would you have expected to give support and food to the Nazis at Stalingrad?" That answer indicates a state of mind that is detrimental to fair and reasonable discussion.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NIGERIA-BIAFRA- ALLEGED FAILURE TO TAKE MEASURES TO RELIEVE STARVATION
speechtext:
I do not mind the noise. Some of the members opposite make their best contributions when they interrupt from a seated position. But they know what is in their hearts. When they go back to their constituencies, they will say that they hope something is going to be done, that they know something will be done. They will say: "We cannot understand why the opposition presses for action, because for 18 months we have been trying to give consideration to this matter. We are giving the question our deepest thought and perchance at some time, somewhere, we will do something".
While this consideration is being given to the matter, tens of thousands of people are
November 27, 1989

dying. They are dying because they have no food. They are dying because some African states say they know better what to do than humanitarian nations in other parts of the world.
No one has explained why this question was not brought before the United Nations. Can any member among those who were interrupting a moment ago tell me why this question has not been put before the United Nations? A year ago last October the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) said: "If we find that that can be done, and it is necessary to be done, we intend to do it".
I want to refer to the record of a number of Canadians, many of them outstanding Liberals, who have been deeply disappointed at the fact that this government has adopted a squalid, nasty, unreasonable and hypocritical attitude to one of the most serious questions of humanitarian need that we have had to face in many years.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
On October 28, 1968, there was an open letter in the Globe and Mail to the Prime Minister on the Nigeria-Biafra war. Under the heading "What is happening?", it reads:
There is general agreement among observers recently returned from Biafra that several thousand civilians are dying every day from starvation. Within weeks this figure will reach tens of thousands when the last stores of bulk food are exhausted. Reporters are equally convinced that even an apparent military victory by the federal troops will not end the fighting since the Biafrans are determined to continue a prolonged guerrilla resistance.
By sending some food and aircraft to Nigeria and Biafra, the Government has shown the Canadian people that it accepts a responsibility for international action where human suffering has reached disastrous proportions.
The open letter has other headings such as "What should be done?", "How can this be done?", "What should Canada do". Under that heading it states:
Canada should greatly increase its efforts in cooperation with like-minded nations to:
have a ceasefire resolution adopted at the United Nations-
Canada refused to place this matter before the United Nations, though it has been asked over and over again.
Secondly, the open letter suggests that there should be a stop in the supply of British arms to Nigeria. I think the strongest objection should have been made by this government to the Wilson Government for supplying
Alleged Failure to Aid Biafrans Nigeria with arms and thereby prolonging the suffering there.
The letter then suggests that we should exert direct and public pressure to end the fighting and re-establish negotiations. This letter was signed by Stephen Clarkson, a Liberal candidate in Toronto for mayor; Allen Linden, chairman of the recent Harrison Hot Springs conference; Marshall McLuhan, the conscience of the Prime Minister; Tim Reid, M.P.P.; Peter Russell, Professor in Toronto and a leading Liberal; Professor John Say-well, who was one of the supporters of the right hon. gentleman for the leadership of the Liberal party; Charles Templeton; Leon Weinstein, the man whom Senator Keith Davey brought forward as a potential nominee for the Liberal party for mayor of Toronto.
They said this question should be brought before the United Nations and many others joined with them. These are outstanding Liberals but what did they get? They simply received, 13 months after they made that declaration, a pious statement by the Prime Minister that there is nothing that can be done- that in effect is what he says-except through assistance from private quarters.
I want to congratulate the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) and the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) on the expression of their viewpoints which they placed fairly before the House.
The attitude of the Government is not that it is marking time but that it is standing still. It is defying the people of Canada openly, overtly and unjustifiably. People ask for action and they receive the reading of an essay on the subject of international relations. I will deal with that in a moment.
We have with us today in this city Mr. Stanley Burke, formerly connected with the CBC. He is a man who gave up his position because of the situation in Biafra and the appeal to his humanitarian sentiments.

speechtext:
We think of the sacrifices of Canadians. Four of these brave men, as a price of their emergency flights, in the month of August, 1969 gave their lives. The Government of Canada dare not continue to defy the hopes and desires of the people of Canada. The Prime Minister can leave. Anyone who runs away lives to speak another day. He can leave, he can evacuate the House, but by his actions today he showed more clearly, more
COMMONS DEBATES	November 27, 1969
Alleged Failure to Aid Biafrans definitely and more assuredly his disregard for this institution which he is endeavouring to remake in the image of the Congressional government of the United States.
What can be done? Toward the end of last year the Biafran authorities completed preliminary surveys for a relief airstrip. In an undertaking with Canairelief and Joint Church Aid, the Biafrans cleared and levelled a strip to be used exclusively for relief purposes. If the Canadian government wishes to send any relief, and certainly the speech of the Prime Minister today indicates no such desire, it could complete this strip easily and quickly by laying down a metal military emergency grid. This could be done in a matter of hours by a military team. Biafran authorities have stated that such action would be deeply appreciated.
Dr. Otue, the senior Biafran representative in New York, is in Ottawa today and has given his personal assurances. Hercules aircraft could thus be flying in food by the hundreds of tons within a matter of days. The food is stockpiled at Sao Tome in thousands of tons. In addition, there are several thousands of tons of Red Cross supplies which have been lying around deteriorating since last June.
Sir, I am shocked by the attitude of the Prime Minister today. He represents all of the people of Canada. He does not want to engage in any dialogue, but would rather have us listen to his monologue. Isn't it about time this Government decided that it should act?
Since June 5, the Red Cross, jointly with Canairelief, has carried into Biafra over 30,000 tons of food, so that in contrast with the negotiations that are going on between the Red Cross and the authorities in Nigeria the population has been assisted to this extent. Canairelief, the Canadian company or group, has just completed its 500th flight. It uses, at the present time, 4 superconstellation planes, and could fly another four flights if additional funds were available. I say to the Government, furnish these funds.
Canadian people are responding well but there are limits. Do you mean to tell me that the Canadian Council of Churches or the other organizations which have joined together for action should be spurned in the way they have been by the expression of the views of this Government today? Why will the Government not contribute to Canairelief?
The Prime Minister today produced a legalistic formula. The request was made in

August and there has been no reply made or there was not up to the day before yesterday. There has been neither a yes nor a no in reply. The Government has hidden behind protocol and pretended international legal principles in order to deny hundreds of thousands of starving people at a time when Canada has the largest surplus of wheat- 1,400 million bushels-in its history. The Government says this cannot be done. Let us simply look at the facts. For a long time the Government said it was unable to get any information from the Nigerian leaders or those associated with them. That was in September and October of 1968.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I decided, as a private member of parliament, to send a message to General Yakubu Gowon, State House, Lagos, Nigeria, imploring him to expedite the clearance of Canadian aircraft to permit relief supplies of food and medicine to be delivered to those parts of Nigeria affected by the civil war. The message continued:
Along with tens of thousands of Canadians I heard you in August in an interview on CBC undertake to assure delivery of relief supplies to the afflicted whatever their political affiliations. The words you used were "I have told you the supplies will get through, I will see to it that it is done". Will you in the name of humanity now do that which you undertook and as a humanitarian assure that innocent children and others in need will secure the available supplies which Canada desires with all its heart to provide.
Within a matter of four days I received a complete answer thereto from Major General Gowon in which he pointed out that he could not understand my message. He said that there is nothing being done on his part or on the part of those associated with him to interfere in any way with food going into Biafra. He said further:
I have at no time failed to honour my pledge to do everything possible to ensure that no one in this country suffered unnecessarily as a result of this war. Unfortunately there are areas to which the authority of my government cannot yet be extended and these are the areas from which the stories of harrowing distress issue but even then my government has made repeated offers of practicable means of getting relief supplies to them. Unfortunately the secessionist leaders have consistently turned down these offers and their supporters in Canada are taking the public for a ride by concealing these facts while parading statistics of the magnitude of distress.
There need be no cause for you to be concerned that relief is not reaching those in need who can be reached. My government is ensuring that more and more of such persons are continuing to be reached.
November 27, 1969

Well, we know what the results are. We know that those statements made by him- although he did answer the request and the plea-were not based on facts. That we know. They tell me the latest excuse is that constitutionally this cannot be done. I have before me a constitutional summary respecting this matter and in particular the right of any country to give humanitarian aid to those who are suffering. Humanitarianism has no protocol.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NIGERIA-BIAFRA- ALLEGED FAILURE TO TAKE MEASURES TO RELIEVE STARVATION
speechtext:
Dr. Edward McWhinney, Q.C., Professor of Law, McGill University, on October 30, 1968 set out in detail the situation. He said there is no constitutional basis for the fatuous excuses being made by the Canadian government in refusing to act. He said further:
-we have heard a number of arguments, legal and otherwise, against using Canadian military planes to transport Red Cross non-military supplies to Biafra. It has been said that that would be a legal act of war; though since the test of a legal act of war, according to both Soviet and Western doctrine, focuses on the purpose to which the activity is directed-here a humanitarian one-this argument is surely legally untenable. Beyond this, a right of humanitarian intervention, limiting the internal sovereignty of any state when it acts contrary to the laws of humanity, has been recognized since the time of Grotius, the founder of modern international law, in the early 17th century. Further, in reaction to the crimes committed during the Hitler era, the World Community has moved decisively to limit the old absolutist claims of national sovereignty, by positive law measures like the Nuremberg War Crimes Tribunal, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and the Genocide Convention itself, thus filling the gaps in the "old" international law. Not merely, therefore, would Canada or any other country seeking to have the UN General Assembly discuss the Nigeria-Biafra conflict not violate Nigeria's claimed sovereignty: in fact, we would be fulfilling a positive duty cast upon all members of the World Community, under the "new" international law created since the downfall of the Nazi regime, to bring up alleged violations of human rights for public discussion in the United Nations.

The Prime Minister says quite rightly that all the compassion is not on the benches of the opposition. Whoever suggested it was? No member on this side of the House has any doubt that all members of the government are as concerned, are as decent, and are as willing to help as is any member of this House or any other citizen of Canada. But that is not the question. The question is that the government is in a position to do something and is refusing to do it. That is the question. Protestations of compassion, protestations of concern or self-righteous and selfserving assurances of a guilty heart do not feed a single baby in Biafra. This merely disgusts those who want to see some action taken. I say this because the Prime Minister gave us a series of excuses which I, for one, cannot accept. What we are saying to the Prime Minister and to the government in this resolution today-and it has been put very eloquently and simply-I can put in one sentence. Since June of this year the flights of the International Red Cross have not taken place those flights ceased last June.
[DOT] (5.20 p.m.)
Since June of this year the only aid to the starving people of Biafra has come through Joint Church Aid and Canairelief, and it is fatuous, callous and distressing for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to sit there and tell us-despite the fact that the only assistance that Biafrans have received since June of this year has been assistance through these church agencies-that he will not help them because he thinks Lagos will not approve. That is precisely what he said. He did not say that Lagos had been asked and has refused. He did not say that anyone from his office had gone to Lagos and said: "we want to help Canairelief. Can we, as a friendly nation, have your agreement to that?" He said that this government in Canada, in a straight jacket of heartless protocol, decided that it cannot undertake this help through Canairelief because of the possibility that Lagos may disapprove.
This is the issue before the House.

House asked the Prime Minister of the Canadian government to intervene? We asked him to help save lives. If that is intervention, then it is about time we intervened. When you are in a situation where there are two sides in a conflict, one side of which, Nigeria, has a mass of territory, an approach from the water and most of the air space, while the other side, Biafra, is a little enclave with a blockade by land and a blockade by water so that food cannot be brought in in any other way than by assistance from the world, what protocol should prevent a civilized society such as Canada from offering that assistance?
If the Canadian government informed Lagos that it had decided to give direct assistance to Canairelief, in view of the fact that no other assistance is available to the Bia-frans, I do not believe for a moment that General Gowan would dare object to that simple humanitarian act by Canada.

Even if we obtained agreement to daylight flights, is it sensible to suggest that night flights be ended? Can one possibly deliver enough assistance to the starving millions in Biafra? Is it wrong to continue night flights, even when there are daylight flights? I do not know what the Prime Minister is talking about when he speaks about agreements, unless he refers to the copies of agreements which I hold in my hand. One of them was made on August 27, 1969 between the Biafran authorities and the International Red Cross. This agreement laid down certain rules. Let me read the introduction, which is as follows:
With reference to the note dated August 1, 1969 from the International Committee of the Red Cross to General Odumegwu Ojukwu, Head of State of Biafra, the ICRC proposes the following modalities.
I am informed, I am sure accurately, that these modalities were all accepted by General Ojukwu on August 27, 1969. They provide for controllers from neutral states approved by Lagos, controllers from neutral states approved by Biafra, and Red Cross participation in watching these flights and what goes into the planes.

Perhaps there is something in his file that we lesser mortals have not seen, but I do not know what he is talking about. I do know there is a signed agreement between the ICRC and Lagos which was arrived at some time after the agreement with Biafra. As I piece the situation together-and my inquiries suggest that I am piecing them together accurately-the International Red Cross went to Biafra and obtained agreement on the modalities which it proposed. It then went to Lagos to get similar agreement from Nigeria, and Nigeria refused to agree to the ICRC proposals and made its own demands.

Cargo and personnel aboard the relief aircraft shall be controlled at the ICRC operational base by
